content: Dill, scientifically known as Anethum graveolens, is an annual herbaceous plant that has a relatively short lifespan. It is native to regions of Southwest and Central Asia. This plant is the only species within the genus Anethum, although some botanists classify it under the related genus Peucedanum, naming it Peucedanum graveolens. Dill typically grows to a height of 40 to 60 centimeters, featuring slender stems and finely divided, soft, delicate leaves that measure 10 to 20 centimeters in length. The ultimate divisions of its leaves are 1 to 2 millimeters wide, which are slightly broader than the threadlike leaves of fennel, which are less than 1 millimeter wide and have a firmer texture. The flowers of dill are small, arranged in umbels with a diameter of 2 to 9 centimeters, and range in color from white to yellow. Its seeds are 4 to 5 millimeters long and 1 millimeter thick, with a straight to slightly curved shape and a longitudinally ridged surface. Dill seeds are commonly used as a spice, while its fresh leaves (referred to as dill) and dried leaves (known as dill weed) are utilized as herbs. Dill originated in Central Asia. According to Zohary and Hopf, wild and weedy varieties of dill are widespread across the Mediterranean basin and West Asia. Although sprigs of dill were discovered in the tomb of Amenhotep II, the earliest archaeological evidence of its cultivation dates back to late Neolithic lakeshore settlements in Switzerland. Additionally, traces of dill have been found in Roman ruins in Great Britain. In Semitic languages, dill is referred to as Shubit. The Talmud specifies that tithes must be paid on the seeds, leaves, and stems of dill. The Bible mentions that Pharisees were in the habit of tithing dill (Matthew 23:23), and Jesus Christ is said to have rebuked them for focusing on tithing dill while neglecting mercy. The name dill is believed to have originated from the Norse or Anglo-Saxon word dylle, which means to soothe or to lull, reflecting the plant's carminative properties that help relieve gas. In some English-speaking countries, dill is occasionally referred to as Dillby. In certain Asian languages, it is known as Shepu or Sowa. Fresh and dried dill leaves, sometimes called dill weed to distinguish them from dill seeds, are used as herbs. Similar to caraway, dill's fern-like leaves are aromatic and are used to flavor various foods, including gravlax (cured salmon), borscht, other soups, and pickles. Dill is considered best when used fresh, as it rapidly loses its flavor when dried. However, freeze-dried dill leaves retain their flavor relatively well for a few months. During the Middle Ages, dill was believed to offer protection against witchcraft. Dill seeds are used as a spice and have a flavor similar to caraway. Additionally, dill oil can be extracted from the plant's leaves, stems, and seeds. Medicinally, dill is recognized as an effective herb for treating colic, gas, and indigestion. For successful cultivation, dill requires warm to hot summers with high levels of sunlight, as even partial shade can significantly reduce its yield. The plant thrives in rich, well-drained soil. Dill seeds remain viable for 3 to 10 years. When cultivating dill for seed production, it should not be grown near fennel, as the two species can hybridize. The seeds are harvested by cutting the flower heads from the stalks when the seeds begin to ripen. The seed heads are then placed upside down in a paper bag and left in a warm, dry location for about a week. Once dried, the seeds easily separate from the stems and can be stored in an airtight container.
